title: {{NAME}} and the Starfall Meadow
moral: When ancient and magical things trust each other, even the most broken places can bloom again.

pages.content: The Starfall Meadow had not bloomed in three hundred years, and you could feel the silence of that long waiting in the air, heavier than ordinary silence, like wool soaked in rain. {{NAME}} walked into it at dusk, his cornflower boots dark with the dew of the long grass, and stood at the heart of an enormous circle of ash. In the centre of the circle, a single cracked geode lay open to the sky, its inner crystal gone dark. Where the crystal had been, there was only absence, a cup-shaped hollow that smelled faintly of something sweet and long extinguished. Around the meadow's edge, barely visible in the blue dusk, stood the silhouettes of animals who had been coming here every evening for generations, waiting for something that never came. A family of hares. A stooped brown bear. Two nervous deer. And on the far side of the circle, immense and still as a statue, a young sauropod with scales like polished slate, her long neck arched downward toward the cracked geode as if she had been watching it all her life.

pages.content: She arrived at the speed of starlight. One moment the meadow had only one kind of magic in it, ancient and sleeping; the next it had two. The unicorn stepped out of the treeline like something deciding to be visible, her coat the colour of new snow caught in firelight, her spiral horn a deep rose-gold that pulsed with its own slow rhythm. Her name was Calla, and she was young for a unicorn, which meant she had only been walking the earth for forty years or so, and was still making excellent discoveries about it. She stopped in front of {{NAME}} and regarded him with violet eyes that held the patience of the very old and the curiosity of the very young, simultaneously. She lowered her horn and touched it to the empty geode. Nothing happened. She raised her head and looked at {{NAME}} steadily, as if suggesting, with great politeness, that perhaps the solution required more than one ingredient. {{NAME}}'s eyes moved from the unicorn to the geode to the sauropod across the circle. Something clicked quietly in his mind.

pages.content: {{NAME}} moved quickly. The sauropod, whose name was Murl and who had the unhurried grace of a creature who has lived through several geological eras, needed coaxing forward. She was shy of the unicorn's light, taking small, careful steps that seemed comical given her size. {{NAME}} walked beside her, one hand resting lightly against her great slate flank, and she matched her pace to his like a ship keeping station with a smaller boat. The bear watched them. The hares pressed together. The deer were absolutely motionless. When Murl's great neck arched over the geode from one side and Calla's glowing horn touched it from the other, something extraordinary happened, or began to. A single crystal filament of light appeared in the geode's hollow, thread-fine and trembling, the exact colour of the sky at the precise moment before dawn when it cannot decide whether it is still night. Then another filament. And another. They were weaving themselves, growing upward like the fastest, most deliberate plant in the history of the world.

pages.content: The crystal grew until it was the height of a small tree, and then it bloomed. There was no other word for it. Petals of cold blue light unfolded outward in slow, sweeping arcs, and wherever they touched the ash circle, flowers erupted: real ones, white and gold and violet, pushing through the dead grey earth in fast-forward, lifting their faces to a light that was neither sun nor moon but something older and cleaner than either. The animals moved without thinking, simply walking forward into the blooming circle, drawn in the same way a cold hand moves toward a warm fire. Murl lowered her head and breathed in the flowers, her enormous nostrils flaring, and made a sound so deep and low it was less heard than felt in the chest. Calla stepped back, her horn dimming slowly to a gentle pulse, watching Murl with those patient violet eyes. {{NAME}} stood in the centre of it all, ankle-deep in the sudden white and gold flowers, and felt the silence of the meadow change, transformed from something heavy into something simply still, the way a held breath becomes an exhale.

pages.content: The meadow settled into its new warmth as the full dark arrived, the crystal tree glowing steadily, throwing soft blue light across the faces of every animal gathered there. Murl folded herself down into the flowers with the architectural complexity of a crane being stored, and several hares immediately decided that the warm space beneath her great neck was an excellent place to sleep. The bear sat with the deer in a way that suggested old acquaintances reunited after a long separation. Calla stood at the edge of the light, her eyes half-closed, her horn barely glowing now, a nightlight left on for comfort. {{NAME}} lay in the deep flowers, looking up through the crystal light at the stars appearing above. The flowers were warm as a quilt around him. The meadow hummed with something that was the opposite of that old heavy silence, it was simply alive. His breathing slowed. His eyes closed. The last thing he heard was Murl, very faintly, humming again, lower and softer, the sound of the earth remembering something it had almost forgotten. What else, {{NAME}} wondered in the last moment before sleep, had this meadow been waiting to give back?
